Projects in Claude: how to organize your company's documents for consistent responses. When your team works with Claude on several client accounts or several departments at the same time, a single generic conversation thread quickly becomes unclear because the assistant no longer knows which document belongs to which subject.

The Projects feature solves precisely this problem by providing a separate space for each topic. Below, we explain what a project contains, which documents are worth uploading to it and how to organize it without turning everything into one chaotic repository.

Projects in Claude: how to organize your company's documents for consistent responses

Claude's projects, referred to as projects in Claude, are workspaces dedicated to a subject, with their own documents, instructions and conversation history. Instead of re-entering your company's context every time, you upload it once to the project, and every new conversation started there already has it available.

The exact availability of this feature changes over time across plans, so check in the application, in your account menu, that the Projects option is active before building an entire workflow around it.

What a project is and how it differs from a regular conversation

A regular conversation with Claude starts empty and remains isolated: what you discussed in a chat yesterday does not influence today's chat unless you copy it manually. A project changes this pattern because everything you upload to it remains available to any new conversation started within the same project.

In practice, a project consists of three parts: a collection of documents called the project's knowledge base, a set of custom instructions that apply automatically and the list of conversations held within it. The three parts work together, not separately.

The difference is felt most by teams working with multiple clients or brands. Without separate projects, every new conversation requires you to explain the brand's tone, target audience or internal rules again, which consumes time and produces variations between responses.

The benefit grows over time, not only in the first conversation. After a few months, a well-maintained project already contains the answer to most repetitive questions about that client or department, and a new colleague gets up to speed much faster than by reading entire folders of separate documents.

How to start a new project, step by step

Starting a project takes a few minutes, but the order of the steps matters for how useful it is from the very first conversation. A project started in a hurry, with documents thrown into it without order, requires more corrective work later than ten minutes of preparation would have required.

  1. Name the project clearly after the client or department it belongs to, not generically "Project 1" or "New".
  2. Write the project instructions first, before uploading documents, so you already have a clear idea of the tone and format you want.
  3. Upload a small initial set of core documents, not the company's entire archive in one go.
  4. Test the project with a real question, one that frequently comes up for that client or department.
  5. Adjust the instructions based on the first response, then gradually add the rest of the necessary documents.

This pattern prevents precisely the mistake described below: a project overloaded from the start with documents that no one has time to check before uploading.

What to put in a project's knowledge base

The knowledge base is where you upload the documents you want Claude to read before answering any question in that project. You do not need to paste them into every message, because they remain attached to the project until you delete or replace them.

For a service business, useful documents vary by project, but several categories consistently recur:

  • Brand guide: tone, prohibited words, forms of address, just like internal editorial rules.
  • Product or service sheets with up-to-date prices and features, not old versions left in the archive.
  • Examples of already approved content as a model for the desired format of new texts.
  • A glossary of company- or industry-specific terms so they do not need to be explained from scratch every time.
  • Templates for recurring documents, such as proposals, reports or standard responses to frequently asked questions.

Old documents or those contradicted by newer versions must be removed from the project, not simply supplemented with others on top. Claude does not know which version is valid if the knowledge base contains two different price sheets for the same service.

Custom instructions for a consistent tone

Alongside documents, each project allows its own set of instructions, valid for all conversations started within it. Here, you write things such as who the texts are intended for, which tone to use, what to avoid and the format in which the response should be delivered, for example directly in HTML or as a bullet-point list.

These instructions are not repeated in every message, which distinguishes them from a regular prompt. You write them once, and Claude applies them automatically while you remain in the same project, as we have already shown in the blog's Claude prompt examples, but at the level of an entire project rather than an isolated message.

For a company, project instructions are the equivalent of a brief handed to a new colleague once, valid for the whole collaboration, not just the first task.

How to organize projects in a small business

A common mistake is one enormous project with documents from all departments mixed together. The result is precisely the problem projects are meant to solve: responses that mix incompatible information.

A more useful structure separates projects along the natural boundaries of the company's work, rather than whatever is easiest to create quickly:

  • One project for each client, with their brand sheets, tone and the history of conversations held for them.
  • One project for internal marketing, separate from client projects, so your own content does not get mixed with content delivered to others.
  • One project for internal technical documentation, useful for the team writing procedures or answering repetitive tickets.
  • One project for research, containing raw materials, notes and data exports, separate from final-content projects.

The practical rule is simple: if two sets of documents should never be mixed in a single response, they belong in different projects. Companies already doing keyword research with Claude quickly notice the benefit, because exports in a research project remain available for all subsequent analyses within that same project.

Projects shared with your team

On plans designed for teams, a project can be shared with several colleagues, who see the same documents and instructions. This means a new colleague gains access to a client's full context through a single invitation, rather than a series of verbal explanations.

Conversations started by different colleagues in the same project use the same knowledge base but generally remain separate discussion threads. Check the project's settings in the application to see exactly who is allowed to add or delete documents, especially in projects containing sensitive client data.

In a company with several collaborators, it is worth deciding beforehand who is responsible for keeping each shared project tidy; otherwise, documents accumulate without anyone checking them. The same person can also maintain a short list outside Claude showing which project corresponds to which client or department, particularly useful as the team grows.

For technical teams that use Claude Code alongside the regular application, organizing by project helps there too, because relevant technical documentation stays linked to the right project instead of scattered across separate conversations.

What to check before uploading documents to a project

Documents uploaded to a project move beyond the strict confines of a single conversation and remain accessible to anyone with access to that project, including colleagues added later. For this reason, several checks are worth making beforehand, not afterward.

Before uploading a document to a project, check these points.

  • The document does not contain third parties' personal data without a legal basis for processing it this way.
  • The people with access to the project genuinely need the content of that document.
  • The uploaded version is current, not an old draft left from another stage.
  • The client contracts allow their documents to be used in an artificial intelligence tool.

The last point matters more than it may seem at first. Some collaboration contracts explicitly prohibit passing client documents through third-party tools, and a Claude project shared with the team falls squarely into this category.

Common mistakes when organizing projects

Alongside the mixing of subjects described above, several habits quickly damage the usefulness of a project that started well:

  • Uploading dozens of documents at once without removing outdated versions, making it impossible to track what is valid.
  • Overly general project instructions such as "write professionally", which are no more helpful than having none.
  • A single project used by the whole company for every subject, effectively undoing the separation the feature provides.
  • No responsible person to periodically remove expired documents from active projects.
  • Creating a new project for every small task instead of reusing an existing project that already covers the same subject.

A tidy project with a few current documents produces better responses than an overstuffed project containing everything the company has ever written. The quality of the knowledge base matters more than its size.

Organizing projects correctly is a simple step, but one with a direct effect on how quickly your team produces consistent content.
